cards.text: Welcome to Psalm 1, baker, the very first song in the whole book of Psalms. It opens with one word: "Blessed." Then it starts describing the man who is blessed, beginning with three things he does NOT do.
He doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked, set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers. He skips all three. Me? I can't even skip ONE spoonful of my own cookie dough.

cards.question: Psalm 1's blessed man won't walk, set foot or sit with certain people. What is the psalm keeping him away from?

answers.text: Traveling too far from his home
Resting before his work is done

cards.text: So that's what he stays away from. Now the psalm flips it with one little word: "But."

cards.question: Instead of the counsel of the wicked, the blessed man's ___ is in the Law of the LORD.
True or false: In Psalm 1, the blessed man thinks on God's law only on the Sabbath.

cards.text: Day and night, friend, not a quick peek between the first snooze and the SECOND snooze. Then the psalm paints a picture: this man is like a tree.

cards.question: Psalm 1 says the blessed man is like a tree. Where is that tree planted?

cards.text: That tree yields its fruit in season, right on time. Which is more than I can say for me and my oven timer.

cards.question: True or false: Psalm 1 says the tree's leaf withers when the dry season comes.
Like that tree, the blessed man in Psalm 1 ___ in all he does.

cards.text: Then four words hit like a slammed oven door: "Not so the wicked!"

cards.question: The blessed man is like a tree by the water. Psalm 1 says the wicked are the opposite. What are they like?

answers.text: Chaff driven off by the wind
A vine climbing up a wall

cards.text: The tree has roots by the water, but chaff has nothing holding it down. One gust and it's GONE, like the flour on my counter the second I sneeze.
Then the psalm says "Therefore," and looks ahead to the judgment.

cards.question: What does Psalm 1 say about the wicked in the judgment?

answers.text: They will be given more time
They will stand with the righteous

cards.question: True or false: Psalm 1 says sinners will have a place in the assembly of the righteous.

cards.text: Last line, friend. Two roads, and the psalm tells you where each one ends up.

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 1, the LORD guards the path of the righteous.
The LORD guards the path of the righteous, but in Psalm 1 the way of the wicked will ___.

findings.problem: This is not the opening card, but it runs to four sentences: the retelling, 'He skips all three,' 'Me?' and the cookie-dough joke. It needs to be shortened to one or two sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This is a near-verbatim cloze of 'his delight is in the Law of the LORD,' asking for the unseen BSB word 'delight.' The preceding card supplies only the word 'But,' so the baker is being asked to supply the line's wording rather than work out an idea already established in the retelling.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The baker has not yet been told that the man meditates on the law 'day and night'; that context arrives only on card 7, after this question. Nothing in the earlier cards establishes whether the made-up 'only on the Sabbath' statement is true, so this becomes an uninformed true-or-false guess.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The card turns the final clause of Psalm 1:3 into a near-verbatim cloze, asking for the unseen BSB wording 'prospers' in '___ in all he does.' This tests the next word of the psalm's line rather than a meaning expressed apart from its exact wording.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card uses both the tree by the water from Psalm 1:3 and the chaff driven by the wind from Psalm 1:4, but it cites only Psalm 1:4. Its citation should cover the verses it actually uses, beginning at Psalm 1:3.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: This reproduces nearly all of Psalm 1:6 and asks for its final unseen word, 'perish.' It is therefore a next-word cloze of the BSB line rather than a question about the verse's movement or meaning.
